title: World Climates & Biomes
description: Why climate varies around the world and how it shapes the great biomes — polar lands, tropical rainforests and hot deserts.

notes.heading: 📌 Weather, Climate and Climate Zones
notes.body: Weather is the day-to-day state of the atmosphere — rain, wind, sunshine, temperature. Climate is the average weather of a place measured over at least 30 years. The world can be divided into broad climate zones based mainly on temperature and rainfall: equatorial (hot and wet all year, near the equator), tropical (hot with a wet and a dry season), arid (very dry — the deserts), Mediterranean (hot dry summers, mild wet winters), temperate (moderate temperatures and rainfall all year, like the UK), and polar (very cold and dry all year). Mountain areas have their own highland climates. Climate zones follow lines of latitude roughly in bands, because latitude is the strongest single control on temperature.

notes.heading: 🔑 What Controls Climate
notes.body: Several factors combine to give each place its climate. Latitude: the Sun's rays hit the equator directly and are concentrated on a small area, but near the poles the same energy is spread over a larger area and passes through more atmosphere — so temperatures fall as you move away from the equator. Altitude: temperature drops by roughly 6.5 degrees C for every 1,000 m climbed, because the thinner air holds less heat — which is why high mountains can be snow-capped even at the equator. Distance from the sea: water heats and cools slowly, so coastal places have milder, smaller temperature ranges than inland ones (this is called continentality). Ocean currents: warm currents (like the North Atlantic Drift reaching the UK) warm nearby coasts, while cold currents cool them and often bring drought. Prevailing winds: winds blowing from the sea bring rain; winds from inland bring dry conditions. Aspect: south-facing slopes (in the northern hemisphere) are warmer and sunnier than north-facing ones.

notes.heading: 📎 Biomes: Ecosystems at a Global Scale
notes.body: A biome is a very large-scale ecosystem — a global community of plants and animals adapted to a particular climate. Because climate controls which plants can grow, and plants support the animals, the map of world biomes closely matches the map of climate zones. The major biomes are: tropical rainforest (equatorial), savanna grassland (tropical, with wet and dry seasons), hot desert (arid), temperate deciduous forest, temperate grassland, Mediterranean scrub, coniferous forest or taiga (cold northern forests), tundra (treeless polar lands), and polar ice. Within each biome, living things show adaptations — special features that help them survive the local climate, such as a cactus storing water or a polar bear's thick fur. Biomes are also interconnected systems: if the climate changes, or humans remove the vegetation, the whole food web is affected.

notes.heading: 🔑 Polar Lands: Cold, Fragile Environments
notes.body: Polar lands (the Arctic around the North Pole and Antarctica around the South Pole) have a cold, dry climate: temperatures stay below freezing for much of the year and precipitation is so low — under 250 mm a year, mostly as snow — that they are sometimes called cold deserts. Winters have months of darkness and summers have months of continuous daylight. In the tundra, the subsoil is permanently frozen (permafrost), which stops deep roots and drainage, so only low-growing mosses, lichens and dwarf shrubs survive the short summer. Animals are highly adapted: polar bears have thick insulating fur and fat, small ears to reduce heat loss and white camouflage; many birds migrate to escape the winter. Indigenous peoples such as the Inuit have traditionally adapted through clothing, housing and seasonal hunting. Polar environments are fragile: food chains are short, plants grow painfully slowly, and damage (from oil exploration, tourism or pollution) takes decades to recover. Climate change is melting sea ice faster here than anywhere else, and Antarctica is protected for science by the Antarctic Treaty.

notes.heading: 🔑 Tropical Rainforests: Layers and Biodiversity
notes.body: Tropical rainforests grow along the equator — the Amazon in South America, the Congo Basin in Africa and South-East Asia — where the climate is hot (around 27 degrees C all year) and wet (over 2,000 mm of rain a year), with daily convectional rainfall: the Sun heats the ground, moist air rises, cools and condenses into afternoon storms. The forest grows in distinct layers. The emergent layer is a few giant trees rising to 60 m; the canopy is a continuous leafy roof at 20-40 m where most life is found; the under-canopy is shaded and humid; the forest floor is dark, so little grows there and dead matter rots fast. Rainforests cover about 6% of the land surface but hold over half of all plant and animal species — extraordinary biodiversity — and provide oxygen, medicines and a store of carbon. Surprisingly, the soil is poor: heavy rain washes nutrients away (leaching), so almost all nutrients are locked up in the living plants and recycled rapidly when leaves fall and decompose.

notes.heading: ⚠️ Deforestation in the Rainforest
notes.body: Deforestation is the clearing of forest, and it is happening fastest in the tropics. Causes include commercial logging for hardwood timber, clearing land for cattle ranching and plantations (palm oil, soya), subsistence slash-and-burn farming by local people, mining for minerals and building roads and dams. Local effects: the nutrient cycle breaks — without trees, heavy rain washes the thin soil away (soil erosion), rivers silt up and flood more, and the local climate becomes drier. Global effects: burning and rotting trees release stored carbon dioxide, adding to climate change, while fewer trees means less CO2 is absorbed; countless species are pushed towards extinction, including plants that might have yielded new medicines. It also displaces indigenous peoples who have lived in the forest for thousands of years. Solutions being tried include selective logging and replanting, national parks and reserves, ecotourism that makes the living forest worth money, international agreements, and debt-for-nature swaps. The key challenge is balancing the economic needs of poor countries against the global value of the forest.

notes.heading: 📎 Hot Deserts: Life with Almost No Water
notes.body: Hot deserts such as the Sahara, Arabian and Australian deserts are found roughly 30 degrees north and south of the equator, where sinking dry air creates high pressure and almost no rain — under 250 mm a year. Skies are clear, so days are scorching (over 40 degrees C) but nights can be bitterly cold because the heat radiates away — a huge daily temperature range. Plants adapt by storing water (cacti have swollen stems, spines instead of leaves to cut water loss, and wide shallow roots), and animals are often nocturnal or burrow underground to escape the heat — the fennec fox's huge ears radiate heat away. People adapt too: nomadic herders move with their animals to find grazing, and traditional light, loose clothing and thick-walled houses keep people cool. Deserts also offer opportunities: sunshine makes them ideal for solar power, oil and minerals lie beneath many deserts, tourists come for the spectacular scenery, and irrigation (where water can be found) allows farming. Challenges include extreme heat, water scarcity and remoteness, which makes development expensive.

flashcards.definition: The average weather conditions of a place measured over a long period, usually at least 30 years.
flashcards.example: The Sahara has a hot, arid climate even though its weather varies from day to day.

flashcards.definition: Distance north or south of the equator; the strongest control on temperature because the Sun's rays are most concentrated near the equator.
flashcards.example: Singapore (near the equator) is hot all year, while northern Norway (high latitude) has long, freezing winters.

flashcards.definition: A continuous movement of ocean water; warm currents heat nearby coasts and cold currents cool them.
flashcards.example: The North Atlantic Drift keeps the UK's winters much milder than places at the same latitude in Canada.

flashcards.definition: A very large-scale ecosystem of plants and animals adapted to a particular climate, such as tropical rainforest or tundra.
flashcards.example: The map of world biomes closely matches the map of climate zones.

flashcards.definition: Ground that stays permanently frozen below the surface, found in polar and tundra regions.
flashcards.example: Permafrost in the tundra stops trees rooting deeply, so only mosses, lichens and dwarf shrubs grow.

flashcards.definition: The tallest layer of a tropical rainforest — a few giant trees rising up to 60 m above the canopy.
flashcards.example: Eagles and bats live in the emergent layer, high above the continuous roof of the canopy.

flashcards.definition: The continuous roof of interlocking tree crowns in a rainforest, about 20-40 m up, where most of the forest's life is found.
flashcards.example: Monkeys, sloths and thousands of insect species spend their whole lives in the canopy.

flashcards.definition: Rain caused when the Sun heats the ground, warm moist air rises, then cools and condenses into towering storm clouds — typical of equatorial afternoons.
flashcards.example: In the Amazon it rains most afternoons as warm air rises and condenses into heavy thunderstorms.

flashcards.definition: The permanent clearing of forest for farming, logging, mining or settlement, with local and global consequences.
flashcards.example: Clearing Amazon rainforest for cattle ranching releases stored carbon and destroys habitats.

flashcards.definition: The variety of plant and animal species in an area; tropical rainforests have the highest biodiversity on Earth.
flashcards.example: A few hectares of rainforest can contain more tree species than the whole of Europe.

flashcards.definition: Extremely dry — a climate with less than about 250 mm of rainfall per year, as in hot deserts.
flashcards.example: The Atacama Desert is so arid that some weather stations have never recorded rain.

flashcards.definition: A special feature of a plant or animal that helps it survive in the conditions of its biome.
flashcards.example: A cactus stores water in its swollen stem and has spines instead of leaves to reduce water loss.

questions.stem: What is the difference between weather and climate?
choices: They mean the same thing
Weather is day-to-day atmospheric conditions; climate is the average weather over at least 30 years
Climate changes daily; weather is measured over decades
Weather only means temperature; climate only means rainfall
questions.explanation: Weather describes what the atmosphere is doing now or this week. Climate is the long-term average pattern, calculated over 30 years or more.

questions.stem: Why are temperatures generally highest near the equator?
choices: The equator is closer to the Sun
The Sun's rays strike the equator directly and are concentrated on a small area
There is more ocean at the equator to store heat
The Earth spins fastest at the equator, creating friction
questions.explanation: At the equator the Sun's rays hit the surface almost straight on, so their energy is concentrated. Near the poles the same energy is spread over a larger area and passes through more atmosphere, so it is colder.

questions.stem: A mountain at the equator is 4,000 m high. Roughly how much colder is its summit than the lowland around it?
choices: About 4 degrees C colder
About 10 degrees C colder
About 26 degrees C colder
The same temperature — mountains at the equator are always warm
questions.explanation: Temperature falls by roughly 6.5 degrees C per 1,000 m of altitude. At 4,000 m that is 4 x 6.5 = 26 degrees C colder, which is why equatorial peaks can be snow-capped.

questions.stem: The UK and central Canada lie at similar latitudes, but UK winters are much milder. What is the main reason?
choices: The UK is at a lower altitude
A warm ocean current (the North Atlantic Drift) heats the UK's coasts, while inland Canada suffers continentality
The UK gets more direct sunshine
Canada is closer to the Arctic Ocean
questions.explanation: Warm ocean currents carry heat to nearby coasts, and the sea's slow cooling keeps coastal winters mild. Inland locations far from the sea experience much more extreme temperatures.

questions.stem: Which biome is a large-scale ecosystem with its own climate, plants and animals?
choices: A single pond
A biome such as the tropical rainforest
A city park
A farmer's field
questions.explanation: A biome is a global-scale ecosystem — like rainforest, desert or tundra — whose plants and animals are adapted to a particular climate. Ponds and parks are small local ecosystems.

questions.stem: Why are polar regions sometimes called cold deserts?
choices: They are covered in sand dunes
Their annual precipitation is under about 250 mm, as low as a hot desert
They are the hottest places on Earth
No animals can survive there
questions.explanation: Deserts are defined by dryness, not heat. Polar air is too cold to hold much moisture, so precipitation (mostly snow) is below about 250 mm a year — the same threshold as hot deserts.

questions.stem: In a tropical rainforest, where is most of the wildlife found?
choices: On the forest floor
In the canopy layer
In the soil
Above the emergent layer
questions.explanation: The canopy is the continuous leafy roof 20-40 m up, where sunlight, fruit and flowers are abundant — it supports the greatest concentration of species. The dark forest floor supports relatively little life.

questions.stem: Why are rainforest soils surprisingly infertile despite the dense vegetation?
choices: The trees remove nutrients faster than they are replaced and heavy rain leaches the soil, so nutrients are stored in the living biomass
Farmers have used up all the nutrients
Volcanic rock makes poor soil everywhere in the tropics
The canopy blocks nutrients from the sky
questions.explanation: Heavy rain leaches (washes out) soil nutrients, and dead matter decomposes so fast that nutrients are rapidly reabsorbed by plants. Almost all the nutrients are locked in the living vegetation, not the soil.

questions.stem: Swollen water-storing stems, spines instead of leaves and wide shallow roots are adaptations of plants in which biome?
choices: Tropical rainforest
Tundra
Hot desert
Temperate deciduous forest
questions.explanation: These are classic desert adaptations: storing water, reducing leaf area (spines) to cut water loss, and spreading shallow roots to absorb rare rainfall quickly before it evaporates.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT a cause of tropical deforestation?
choices: Commercial logging for hardwood timber
Clearing land for cattle ranching and palm oil plantations
Building wind turbines to generate electricity
Slash-and-burn subsistence farming
questions.explanation: Logging, ranching, plantations, slash-and-burn farming, mining and road building all clear rainforest. Wind turbines are a renewable energy technology, not a driver of deforestation.

questions.stem: How does deforestation contribute to global climate change?
choices: Burning and rotting trees release stored CO2, and fewer trees remain to absorb CO2 by photosynthesis
Trees release methane when they fall over
Open land reflects less sunlight than forest
Deforestation removes oxygen from the atmosphere
questions.explanation: Forests are a giant carbon store. Clearing and burning them releases that carbon as CO2, while destroying the trees removes a major natural absorber of CO2 — a double blow to the climate.

questions.stem: Why are polar environments described as fragile?
choices: The ice is too thin to walk on anywhere
Short food chains and extremely slow plant growth mean damage takes decades to recover
There are too many species competing for resources
Tourists are banned from visiting them
questions.explanation: In polar regions plants grow extremely slowly and food chains are short and simple, so if vegetation is destroyed or a species declines, the whole ecosystem is disrupted and recovery can take many decades.

questions.stem: Two coastal towns lie 200 km apart: one beside a warm current, one beside a cold current at the same latitude. Which prediction is most likely correct?
choices: They will have identical climates
The warm-current town will be milder and wetter; the cold-current town will be cooler and often drier
The cold-current town will be hotter because cold water creates storms
Ocean currents only affect the sea, never the land
questions.explanation: Warm currents transfer heat to the air above and raise coastal temperatures and rainfall; cold currents chill the air, stabilise it and often produce drought and fog — as along the coast of the Atacama Desert.

questions.stem: A fennec fox has huge ears and is active only at night. What do these adaptations help it cope with in the hot desert?
choices: Finding food in the dark
Losing body heat through the ears and avoiding the extreme daytime heat
Hiding from predators underground
Conserving water by sleeping
questions.explanation: Large ears act like radiators, releasing body heat, and nocturnal behaviour keeps the fox in its burrow during the scorching day — both are ways of coping with extreme desert heat.

questions.stem: A desert government wants to develop its economy sustainably. Which option best matches a hot desert's genuine opportunities?
choices: Large-scale rice farming using river water
Solar power generation, mineral extraction and desert tourism
Commercial forestry for timber exports
Deep-sea fishing
questions.explanation: Hot deserts have exceptional sunshine for solar power, often rich oil and mineral deposits, and spectacular scenery that attracts tourists. Rice farming and forestry need far more water than deserts can supply.
